cards.front: How is volume-load calculated in resistance training, and how does it differ from repetition-volume and mechanical work?
cards.back: Volume-load is calculated by multiplying the weight assigned by the number of repetitions performed and summing these values over a training session (Weight × Repetitions). It reflects total mechanical work and metabolic stress. Unlike repetition-volume (total reps), volume-load quantifies overall resistance workload, though it omits vertical displacement distance. For body-moving movements (e.g., loaded jump squats), system mass volume-load must be calculated: [Body Mass + Load] × Repetitions.

cards.front: What is the fundamental relationship between load and repetitions, and what are the key limitations of relying strictly on %1RM tables?
cards.back:
Load and repetitions share an inverse relationship: heavier loads allow fewer repetitions. Major limitations of %1RM tables (Table 17.7) include:
  • The load-rep relationship is curvilinear, not strictly linear.
  • Trained athletes complete more reps at a given %1RM on lower body core exercises and machine lifts compared to upper body or free weight lifts.
  • Table values reflect a single set; multiple sets cause cumulative fatigue.
  • The table is most accurate for heavy loads (>75% 1RM and <10 repetitions).

cards.front: What athlete prerequisites, exercise selection rules, and protocols govern direct 1-repetition maximum (1RM) testing?
cards.back: Direct 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate and advanced resistance-trained athletes with proper technique experience. It must be conducted only on core multijoint exercises (e.g., back squat, bench press). Exercises where stabilizing muscles fatigue prematurely (e.g., bent-over row) are excluded. Protocols include warm-up sets and load increments of 5–10% (upper body) or 10–20% (lower body) to determine 1RM within 3 to 5 attempts with 2–4 minutes rest.

cards.front: What rules govern multiple-RM testing for estimating 1RM, and why are assistance exercises restricted to an 8RM cap?
cards.back: When 1RM testing is inappropriate, a 10RM test can project 1RM (most accurate for loads ≤10RM and >75% 1RM). However, power exercises must never be tested above 5 repetitions due to rapid technique deterioration. Additionally, multiple-RM testing and load assignments for assistance exercises must be capped at or above an 8RM (≤8RM load) to minimize isolative joint and connective tissue stress.

cards.tag: Load and Repetition Prescriptions by Goal
cards.front: What are the specific load (%1RM), repetition, and set assignments for Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, and Muscular Endurance?
cards.back:
Prescriptions according to Table 17.9:
  • Strength: ≥85% 1RM, ≤6 reps, 2–6 sets.
  • Single-Effort Power: 80–90% 1RM, 1–2 reps, 3–5 sets.
  • Multiple-Effort Power: 75–85% 1RM, 3–5 reps, 3–5 sets.
  • Hypertrophy: 67–85% 1RM, 6–12 reps, 3–6 sets.
  • Muscular Endurance: ≤67% 1RM, ≥12 reps, 2–3 sets.

cards.front: How does the force-velocity curve explain why maximal power output occurs at submaximal loads rather than 1RM loads?
cards.back: Maximal force occurs at slow contraction velocities (1RM), yielding lower power output (Power = Force × Velocity). Peak power output occurs at intermediate movement velocities with submaximal loads. For Olympic weightlifting movements (snatch, clean), power output peaks at 75% to 90% 1RM. Reducing load from 100% to 90% 1RM in squats/deadlifts can double power output due to drastically reduced movement duration.

cards.tag: Submaximal Loading Rule for Power Lifts
cards.front: Why are power exercises assigned submaximal %1RM loads (75–90%) for low reps (1–5 reps) rather than true repetition maximums?
cards.back: Power exercises cannot be loaded to true momentary muscle failure (true RMs) because explosive movement velocity and technique deteriorate before muscular failure occurs. Assigning submaximal loads (e.g., 75–85% 1RM for 3–5 reps) ensures maximal movement speed and explosive motor unit execution without technical breakdown or deceleration.

cards.tag: Microcycle Load Variation (Heavy, Light, Medium Days)
cards.front: How does alternating Heavy, Light, and Medium loading days across a microcycle prevent overtraining while preserving frequency?
cards.back:
To avoid systemic overtraining during high-load phases:
  • Heavy Day: Assigned 100% of target RM load for goal repetitions.
  • Light Day: Assigned 80% of Heavy Day load for the exact same goal repetition count.
  • Medium Day: Assigned 90% of Heavy Day load for the exact same goal repetition count.
Athletes complete only the goal reps on light/medium days even if capable of more.

cards.tag: Progression of Training Load: The 2-for-2 Rule
cards.front: What is the 2-for-2 rule for progressing resistance training loads, and how is it operationally applied?
cards.back: The 2-for-2 rule is a conservative progression strategy: If an athlete can perform two or more repetitions over their assigned repetition goal in the last set of an exercise for two consecutive workouts, weight should be added to that exercise for the next training session.

cards.front: What are the standard recommended absolute and relative load increments when progressing training loads under the 2-for-2 rule?
cards.back:
Recommended absolute load increments (Table 17.10):
  • Smaller/Weaker Athletes: Upper body +2.5 to 5 lb (1–2 kg); Lower body +5 to 10 lb (2–4 kg).
  • Larger/Stronger Athletes: Upper body +5 to 10+ lb (2–4+ kg); Lower body +10 to 15+ lb (4–7+ kg).
Alternatively, relative load increases of 2.5% to 10% can be applied to account for individual status and exercise muscle mass.
